extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and judges (Federal Circuit/district courts)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes substantive and procedural standards used in federal patent litigation (inequitable conduct, unclean hands, damages, willfulness, venue/transfer, disclosure obligations, briefs/word limits, fees). Useful for practitioners evaluating liability, remedies, and litigation conduct under Federal Circuit and district-court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing on this defense requires proof of clear and convincing evidence that the patent applicant 'misrepresented or omitted material information with the specific intent to deceive the PTO.' (quoting Therasense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both materiality and specific intent to deceive must be shown by clear and convincing evidence. Courts examine the applicant's state of mind during the relevant time (e.g., periods of non-response). Evidence of communications or omissions may be insufficient if reasonable explanations (e.g., decisionmakers never received communications) exist that negate deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality in inequitable conduct (affirmative egregious misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Affirmative egregious misconduct' satisfies the materiality requirement for inequitable conduct automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality should be analyzed as a separate requirement from deceptive intent. When conduct is affirmatively egregious (e.g., deliberate filing of false statements, deliberate withholding of critical references), courts may deem materiality satisfied without additional proof; nevertheless intent still must be assessed unless the misconduct itself is dispositive on intent under the court's analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive intent — pattern-of-misconduct inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of misconduct can, as a whole, demonstrate deceptive intent even when each individual act may not do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must analyze misrepresentations in aggregate rather than in isolation for intent. District courts should analyze the intent behind each misrepresentation and consider cumulative behavior; failure to do so can warrant vacatur and remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequivocal standard of proof for inequitable conduct/intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceptive intent must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that could be consistent with innocent explanations (e.g., attorney genuinely believed corporate decisionmakers had not authorized abandonment) will defeat a finding of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean hands — threshold and connection to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine applies where a party engaged in 'deceit and reprehensible conduct . . . to gain an unfair advantage' and the misconduct 'bear[s] an immediate and necessary connection' to the claims for relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates whether conduct was unconscionable and whether it affected litigation of plaintiff's claims. Concealment of relevant applications, false testimony, concealing prior art searches, or other deceit connected to the asserted claims can justify invoking unclean hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of agent misconduct to principal (unclean hands)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent (e.g., former in-house attorneys or affiliated entity) acted as the plaintiff's agent before and during litigation, the agent's misconduct is imputable to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where agents used confidential or privileged information, breached fiduciary duties, lied, spoliated evidence, or took steps to cover up misconduct, courts may attribute that conduct to the principal and deny relief or dismiss with prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for pervasive unclean hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal with prejudice is an appropriate remedy when plaintiff's bad-faith conduct 'infected' the entire case and monetary sanctions would not restore integrity or punish adequately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh severity and pervasiveness of misconduct; where the litigation has been substantially tainted (theft of opponent's privileged/confidential analyses, spoliation, cover-up), dismissal with prejudice may be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: WesternGeco two-step extraterritoriality framework (damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether patent damages can include foreign effects, apply WesternGeco's two-step framework: (1) start with a presumption that the statute lacks extraterritorial reach and determine whether that presumption is rebutted; (2) analyze the statute's 'focus' to determine whether the conduct relevant to that focus is domestic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the relevant conduct is domestic (e.g., acts that constitute infringement under the statute), foreign losses caused by that domestic conduct may be recoverable. The court may apply this framework across different infringement provisions (e.g., §271(a) and §271(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation requirement for including foreign conduct in reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: For reasonable royalty cases, foreign conduct that is not itself infringing must cause the value of the domestic infringement to increase to be included in the damages calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages based on foreign activity are only recoverable if that foreign conduct has a causal effect on the value that domestic infringement creates in the hypothetical negotiation. Courts may leave detailed application of this causation requirement to future cases, but require a clear causal link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility & reliability of reasonable-royalty experts (hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert using the hypothetical negotiation model must tie the proposed royalty rate to facts of the case (e.g., comparable license agreements, market evidence, profit analysis) so that the testimony is sufficiently reliable to be admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the expert's methodology is grounded in case facts (comparable licenses, accounting for discounts, adjustments for portfolio vs single-patent licenses) and whether the expert apportioned value appropriately. Mere 'plucked' rates without factual tie-ins can be excluded; reliance on comparable agreements, market data, and profit-per-unit analyses supports admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment and entire market value rule (EMVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire market value rule may be applied only when the patented feature 'drove market demand' for the entire product; otherwise damages must be apportioned to reflect the value of only the patented improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show that the patented features drove demand (e.g., consumer surveys, market studies). If patented technology is a small component of a larger system, and other conventional factors can drive demand, apportionment is required and EMVR is improper without evidence that the patented feature was the driver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness evidence and 35 U.S.C. §298
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence at trial should not run afoul of §298 by effectively commenting on the accused infringer's decision to seek advice of counsel; experts cannot substitute third-party consulting advice for legal advice of counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony that implies an accused infringer failed to seek advice of counsel can improperly support a willfulness finding contrary to §298. Courts will exclude or discount expert testimony that does not distinguish between legal and non-legal services when arguing that an accused infringer was willful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required for willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove willfulness, plaintiff must show more than knowledge of asserted patents; it must show that defendant knew it was infringing and intended to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence limited to knowledge of patents is insufficient. Courts require evidence showing deliberate or reckless disregard of a known patent right; improper expert testimony about industry practices without linking to legal advice is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue/transfer standard under Fifth Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer 'should be granted if the movant demonstrates that the transferee venue is clearly more convenient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh private and public interest factors: compulsory process (ability to compel nonparty witnesses), local interest (connection to accused technology), willing witness convenience, practical problems, sources of proof, and location of parties/witnesses/evidence. No single factor is dispositive; transferee venue must be 'clearly more convenient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial-economy and 'legitimate mooring' in transfer analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Incremental gains in judicial economy favoring the transferor forum are outweighed if the case lacks a legitimate mooring to that forum (location of parties, witnesses, evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior docket familiarity may be outweighed by more substantial connection of parties, witnesses, or evidence to the transferee forum. Courts must assess the weight of judicial economy versus other convenience factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for transfer (mandamus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit reviews district court transfer denials for clear abuse of discretion and will not disturb transfer decisions unless facts and circumstances are without any basis for a judgment of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandamus relief requires a showing that the district court's denial was a clear abuse of discretion; when several transfer factors favor transfer and none favor the original forum, courts may grant mandamus to correct the district court's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassignment to patent docket/local case management orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a complaint 'involves patents' district courts may apply local reassignment orders that move the case onto the court's patent docket or to particular judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amending a complaint to add patent causes of action can trigger reassignment orders. Attempts to plead around reassignment (e.g., by alleging only antitrust claims) can be defeated by subsequent amendments invoking patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of controlling entities / real parties in interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs must disclose controlling entities and real parties in interest; failure to produce documents about relationships with entities that fund or direct litigation can trigger sanctions and referrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts scrutinize assignments, funding arrangements, profit-sharing, and control (e.g., entities receiving up to 95% of profits). Counsel must communicate with actual clients, address conflicts of interest, and obtain informed consent; failing to do so may violate professional conduct rules and justify referrals to disciplinary authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice and improper delegation of litigation control
rubrics_metrics.description: When in-house or affiliated personnel of a controlling entity perform legal work or direct litigation for nominal plaintiffs who do not share the same interests, that may constitute unauthorized practice of law or other professional violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may refer such conduct to state unauthorized-practice committees or bar disciplinary authorities when individuals working for funding entities appear to be directing litigation or providing legal services to parties without proper authority or disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements to the PTO and potential criminal exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory or false assignments and filings with the USPTO may implicate 18 U.S.C. §1001(a), making it a crime to knowingly submit materially false statements to a federal agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent assignment records or apparent misrepresentations in PTO filings can prompt referral to DOJ or the USPTO for further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's power to compel appearance and contempt for noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can issue sua sponte orders compelling a party representative (e.g., sole owner) to appear for a hearing investigating potential misconduct; refusal to comply can result in civil contempt under the court's inherent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 45 (party-issued subpoenas) does not limit a court's sua sponte power to order appearances. Compelling appearances is appropriate to investigate potential misconduct where the individual is the party's representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference in appellate briefs and word limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may not incorporate by reference arguments from another brief in a way that results in exceeding the applicable word count; incorporation to circumvent word limits is disallowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts enforce word-count limits; incorporating thousands of words from a companion brief that pushes a brief over the limit may be treated as a violation that could result in sanctions. There is no special exception for copying from a party's own companion appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney's fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 — exceptional_case factors
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may award attorney's fees when a case is 'exceptional' based on factors or 'red flags' showing objectively baseless claims or misconduct, but not all adverse developments justify fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant considerations include prior parallel litigation invalidating patents (may be relevant), but PTAB decisions, non-final office actions, unrelated Federal Circuit cases, notice letters, or ordinary expert testimony do not automatically make a case exceptional. Courts must assess the totality of circumstances and whether the plaintiff had reasonable arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverability of IPR-related fees under §285
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney's fees incurred in IPR proceedings are not recoverable under 35 U.S.C. §285 when a defendant voluntarily pursued IPRs in parallel to district-court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit reasoned that awarding IPR fees under §285 would require district courts to evaluate exceptionalness in proceedings they did not oversee and that parties voluntarily electing IPR obtain advantages (lower burdens, efficiency). There is a split in views (dissent argues IPRs can be involuntary in response to a baseless suit), but the prevailing guidance is that IPR fees are generally not recoverable under §285.
